name: Tretinoin protocol (tret, buffering)

lead: The tret protocol is looksmaxxing shorthand for easing into prescription tretinoin and cushioning it with moisturiser, aiming for smoother, clearer, less wrinkled skin with fewer pores and spots.

Tretinoin acts on retinoic acid receptors in skin cells, speeding turnover, normalising follicle keratinisation and, per reports, boosting collagen. It is described as the most extensively studied topical retinoid for photoageing, with studies running up to two years, and is also studied for acne. Buffering is meant to reduce irritation rather than change the mechanism, and reference sources do not describe buffering or slow-ramp schedules specifically.

paras: People start with infrequent use and increase gradually, often layering moisturiser before or after to reduce irritation, typically at night with daily sunscreen by day. Skin changes build over months. It is prescribed in many countries.
Irritation, redness, peeling and sun sensitivity are common. It is contraindicated in pregnancy. It is available by prescription in many countries.

chain: Collagen builds, pores and spots improve
angle.text: Looksmaxxing forums share routines for starting tretinoin slowly and buffering it with moisturiser to reduce irritation, aiming for smoother, clearer, less wrinkled skin. The retinoid speeds skin cell turnover and builds collagen. Tretinoin itself has been studied for acne and photoaging for up to two years.

lead: The tretinoin protocol, usually shortened to "tret" on looksmaxxing forums, is the way people ease into topical tretinoin (all-trans retinoic acid, sold as Retin-A, Avita, Renova and generics) and manage its irritation. Users aim for smoother, clearer, more even-toned and firmer-looking skin, with fewer visible acne marks and fine lines, and many describe starting with infrequent applications that increase as the skin adapts and "buffering" the product with moisturiser.[1][2]

Tretinoin is described as the most extensively studied topical retinoid for photoageing, with studies running up to two years. Topical retinoids are reported to increase collagen production, thicken the epidermis and speed the fading of post-acne dark marks, with visible change typically taking weeks to months.[1] Reference sources note that tretinoin is a prescription medicine in the US, UK, EU and Australia, that irritation, redness, peeling and sun sensitivity are common, and that it is contraindicated in pregnancy.[1]

Buffering itself, meaning applying moisturiser before or over the retinoid, is a community and clinician convention rather than a subject of published trials. Wikipedia's tretinoin article describes gradual introduction (every second or third night at first), waiting after washing the face, and a non-comedogenic moisturiser as management steps for irritation.[1] On forums, users also discuss eyelid use, face-slimming claims, and dose frequency.[3][4][5]
infobox: Prescription-only in the US, UK, EU, Australia[1]

paras: Tretinoin is all-trans retinoic acid. Topical forms (cream, gel, lotion, microsphere gel) are used for acne and for photoaged skin.[1] The "tret protocol" in appearance communities refers to the routine around it: starting at low frequency, raising it as the skin adapts, and layering moisturiser (buffering) to moderate dryness and peeling.[3][4]

Wikipedia's article lists comparable steps as irritation management: beginning every other or every third night, waiting at least 20 minutes after washing and drying the face, and using a non-comedogenic moisturiser if needed.[1] Forum users ask related questions, such as whether moisturiser applied afterwards rubs the medicine off and whether applying a lower strength twice matches a higher strength once.[6][7]

Topical retinoids increase collagen production, thicken the epidermis and reduce abnormal pigment-cell and keratinocyte changes in photoaged skin; improvement takes several weeks to months and has been studied up to two years.[1] Tretinoin also speeds the resolution of post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation after acne, including in darker skin.[1]
Wikipedia's wrinkle article lists tretinoin among topical treatments studied for wrinkles.[2] The retinoid class article describes the group of vitamin A derivatives to which it belongs.[8]

Common topical reactions are irritation, redness, swelling, peeling and, in some cases, blistering; users report increased sun sensitivity, attributed to a thinner stratum corneum and irritation. It should not be applied to the eyes or mucous membranes, and it is contraindicated in pregnancy because of birth-defect risk.[1]

On looksmax.org, one user asked about eyelid application and the risk of dry or red eyes, and another thread carries a warning for tretinoin users about meibomian glands.[3][5] Others report rashes and a very red face during use.[9]

Tretinoin was patented in 1957. James Fulton and Albert Kligman at the University of Pennsylvania developed it for acne in the 1960s, it was approved for medical use in 1962, and the FDA approved it for acne in 1971 as Retin-A.[1] Its use for photoageing later made it a mainstay of cosmetic dermatology; the University of Pennsylvania held the patent and licensed it to manufacturers.[1]

Tretinoin for photoaged skin and acne has been studied in trials running up to two years, and topical retinoids are reported to improve wrinkles, pigmentation and elasticity.[1] No published trials have tested buffering with moisturiser or slow-ramp schedules as defined in forum protocols, and no studies were found on facial fat reduction.
Retin-A is a regular topic on looksmax.org. Threads cover how long a tube lasts, low-dose long-term use, collagen concerns, and whether it affects the nose or cheek fullness.[4][10][11]

One user wrote after six months on tretinoin and a cutting phase that his cheek fat looked flatter and attributed it to both, while noting acne scars looked more visible at first.[4] Another long-term user said he still had forehead lines and crow's feet after years of use.[12]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org tretinoin is discussed as an anti-ageing, skin-quality and face-slimming tool, with threads on strength, frequency and side effects.[4][6][10]
